name: YOUR SWISS IS ON MY LIST BURGER

recipe.history:
Swiss cheese — or more precisely, the family of cheeses that Americans call 'Swiss' — originates in the high alpine meadows and valleys of Switzerland, particularly the Emmental district of the canton of Bern, where cheesemakers have been producing Emmentaler since the 13th century. The characteristic holes, known formally as 'eyes,' form during aging as Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria consume lactic acid and release carbon dioxide gas, which becomes trapped in the semi-hard paste, forming the bubbles that harden into the familiar cavities. Authentic Emmentaler AOP is a massive cheese — wheels weigh 175 to 220 pounds — and requires months of careful aging in mountain cellars. The flavor is mild, nutty, and slightly sweet, with a buttery quality that develops depth with age. Gruyère, also Swiss in origin, from the canton of Fribourg, is the more assertive cousin: smaller holes, denser texture, more complex and earthy flavor that intensifies dramatically with age. Both cheeses melt with exceptional smoothness, making them the foundation of Swiss fondue, one of the world's great communal dishes.

Swiss-style cheese became part of the American cheeseburger tradition largely through the deli sandwich world — the Reuben, the Club, the Monte Cristo — where its mild meltability made it useful across a wide range of applications. The fondue approach applied to a burger — melting Swiss in a fondue-style fashion with white wine and a touch of kirsch, then spooning it warm over the patty — takes the deli tradition and elevates it into something more intentional. The nutty sweetness of the melted Swiss against the savory richness of a beef patty creates a combination that is simultaneously homey and sophisticated. Adding Gruyère to the fondue-style sauce deepens the flavor profile and ensures the sauce has enough character to hold its own against the beef.

I went through a fondue phase in my late twenties after a winter trip to a Swiss-themed restaurant that served fondue in individual earthenware pots with crusty bread and boiled potatoes. I came home and made fondue three weekends in a row, each time adding slightly more Gruyère and slightly less Emmentaler until I found the ratio I liked. One evening I had leftover fondue and a defrosted burger patty and no bread in the house except the brioche rolls I had made that morning, and the decision to pour the fondue over the burger was partly desperation and partly curiosity. It turned out to be one of the better accidents of my cooking life. The warm cheese sauce pooling into the crevices of the patty and soaking into the toasted bun was exactly as good as it sounds.

The medium-rare imperative for this burger is bound up in texture: the warm, flowing Swiss fondue sauce requires a patty that is also yielding and tender, a second layer of soft richness that creates a unified texture in every bite. A well-done patty introduces a hard, dry counterpoint to the silky cheese sauce — the two textures fight each other rather than harmonize. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the beef is still pink and moist, its fat still present in the meat rather than rendered into the pan, and the combination of medium-rare beef with fondue-style Swiss creates a layered richness that is deeply satisfying without being cloying. Restraint in cooking temperature is the same discipline as restraint in seasoning: knowing that less heat, at the right moment, is always more.
ingredients: Coarse pretzel salt or flaky sea salt
For the Swiss fondue burger sauce:
3/4 cup dry white wine (Swiss Chasselas or Sauvignon Blanc)
Fine sea salt and black pepper
instructions: 1. Make the pretzel buns: Combine warm water, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer. Bloom 5 minutes. Add flour, salt, and butter; knead with dough hook 8–10 minutes until smooth. Cover and let rise 1 hour until doubled.
2. Punch down dough, divide into 6 equal balls. Shape tightly. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet; proof 30 minutes.
3. Preheat oven to 425°F. Bring 8 cups water to a boil; add baking soda (it will foam). Boil each bun 30 seconds per side using a slotted spoon. Return to baking sheet.
4. Brush boiled buns with beaten egg; sprinkle with coarse salt. Cut a shallow X on top of each with a sharp knife. Bake 14–16 minutes until deep mahogany brown. Cool on a rack.

5. Make the sautéed mushrooms: Melt butter in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add mushrooms in a single layer; cook without stirring 4 minutes until browned. Add shallot, garlic, and thyme; cook 2 more minutes. Deglaze with white wine; cook until evaporated. Season. Set aside.
6. Form the patties: Combine ground chuck with salt and both peppers. Divide into 4 portions (8 oz each). Shape into 4.5-inch patties with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.

7. Cook the patties: Heat cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes. Flip; cook 2–3 minutes more. Target 130–135°F internal temperature for medium rare. Remove, tent with foil, rest 3 minutes.

8. Make the fondue sauce while patties rest: Rub a small saucepan with the cut garlic, then discard garlic. Add white wine and warm over medium heat until just simmering. Toss grated Gruyère and Emmentaler with cornstarch. Add cheese to wine in three batches, stirring in a figure-8 motion until completely melted between each addition. Stir in kirsch, Dijon, nutmeg, and white pepper. Keep warm over very low heat, stirring occasionally.
9. Quickly wilt spinach in olive oil in a skillet over medium-high heat, 1 minute. Season.
10. Toast pretzel bun halves cut-side down in butter in a skillet until golden, about 90 seconds.

11. Assemble: Place wilted spinach on the bottom bun. Add mushrooms. Place the rested patty. Ladle warm Swiss fondue sauce generously over the top of the patty, allowing it to cascade down the sides. Finish with flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun.
12. Serve immediately with any extra fondue sauce on the side for dipping.
